title: Can God Trust You? A Study of the Parable of the Talents
metaDescription: God is trustworthy, but can He trust you? Explore Jesus' parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30 and learn what it means to be a faithful servant.
bodyHtml:
We know we're supposed to trust God. That's a given for most of us who follow Jesus. But this sermon flips the question in a way that lands with surprising force: God doesn't only want you to trust Him p>

Think about it the way you would a marriage. If a husband said, "My wife fully trusts me, but I don't trust her at all," we'd immediately recognize that something is broken. A healthy relationship requires mutual trust. And if our relationship with God is meant to be real and living, then trust has to flow in both directions. God is perfectly trustworthy But the startling truth is that God, despite our failures, actually wants to trust us with something.

The Parable of the Talents

Closing out our Transformational Stories series through the parables of Jesus, this message walks through Matthew 25:14-30. A master, about to leave on a journey, entrusts his wealth to three servants:

"To one he gave five bags of gold, to another two bags, and to another one bag, each according to his ability. Then he went on his journey." (Matthew 25:15)

Even the servant with one bag was handed a fortune what scholars estimate to be roughly twenty years of wages. Two of the servants put their money to work and doubled it. The third dug a hole and buried what he'd been given. When the master returned, his response to the first two was the same: "Well done, good and faithful servant."

The Kind of Person God Can Trust

So who is the person God can trust? Simply put, the one who faithfully works with what God has given them. The sermon drew out three qualities of a faithful servant.

1. Recognize what God has given you

Every person is entrusted with something bilities, responsibilities, opportunities, relationships, time, and treasure. But notice the servants weren't given equal amounts. You are not called to be faithful with someone else's gifts. The biggest thief of contentment here is comparison. When we're busy envying what others have, we never appreciate r use what God actually placed in our hands.

2. Choose to be dependable

To be faithful is to be dependable o actually do what you say you'll do, consistently, even when you don't feel like it. A car that starts four days out of seven isn't dependable. Faithfulness isn't occasional obedience; it's steady character. What would it look like to be a dependable spouse, parent, giver, or servant showing up when it's hard, not just when it's convenient?

3. Work urgently and strategically

The servant with five bags "went at once" and put the money to work. There was no delay and delayed obedience is really just disobedience. But urgency alone isn't enough. Doubling those resources took planning and wisdom. God wants us to serve Him both promptly and thoughtfully.

Here's the freeing part: the root of fruitfulness is faithfulness. When we obsess over results, we often stall out. When we simply focus on being faithful with what's in front of us, the fruit tends to follow.

The Reward of Faithfulness

When the master returns, the faithful servants say something revealing: "You entrusted me with..." (Matthew 25:20). They understood they were stewards, not owners. Everything they held belonged to the master. When you realize your money, time, and relationships are gifts on loan from God, you live differently.

"Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful with a few things; I will put you in charge of many things." (Matthew 25:23)

Faithfulness with little leads to being trusted with much both in eternity and often here and now. Most of us complain about not having more instead of being faithful with what we already have. But God trusts the servant who quietly goes above and beyond, not the one who does the bare minimum while demanding a promotion.

The Cost of Faithlessness

The unfaithful servant offers a striking example. He didn't lose his one bag he simply kept it buried. Unfaithfulness isn't only about wasting your life; it can be about merely maintaining it while never multiplying it for God's glory and others' good. His reasons? Fear and selfishness. "I was afraid," he said (Matthew 25:25). Fear freezes us it is impossible to be fearful and faithful at the same time. And the master's verdict "you wicked, lazy servant" exposes a heart turned inward.

The parable ends with sobering words about judgment and being cast out. It's a reminder that God is both loving and just, and that these are not weightless matters. But there is enormous hope woven through it, too.

Faithful When We Were Not

The good news is that our story doesn't rest on our faithfulness it rests on His. Paul writes:

"What if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify God's faithfulness? Not at all!... For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus." (Romans 3:3-4, 23-24)

The cross is the clearest picture of God's faithfulness toward unfaithful people. Like Hosea sent to love and redeem a wandering spouse, God pursues us even when we've given our hearts to lesser things. The more we place our faith in the faithful One, the more faithful we become and the more He can trust us with.

A Takeaway to Sit With

So here's the reflection question to carry into your week: How is your heart are you living by fear or by faith, selfishly or sacrificially? And practically: what is the one thing already in front of you that God is asking you to be faithful with right now?

If these questions are stirring something in you, we'd love to walk with you. Arroyo Church is a Bible-teaching family in Livermore and the greater Tri-Valley, and there's a place for you here. Come as you are.
